sections.title: What You'll Learn
sections.content:
Ever wondered why 2 + 3 * 4 equals 14 and not 20? Let's crack the code of operator precedence and associativity!

• How Java decides which operation to do first
• The secret order of math operations (PEMDAS for coders!)
• How to use parentheses to take control of evaluation

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
Imagine you're at a buffet with different food stations. The dessert station (parentheses) gets served first, no matter where it's placed in line. Then comes the main course (multiplication/division), and finally the appetizers (addition/subtraction).

Java follows similar rules when evaluating expressions:

• **Parentheses first**: Just like dessert, expressions in parentheses get top priority
• **Multiplication/Division**: These have higher precedence than addition/subtraction
• **Left-to-right**: When operators have equal precedence, Java works left to right

For example: `3 + 4 * 2` equals 11, not 14, because multiplication happens before addition!

sections.title: Code Examples
Key Points
points: Unary operators (!, ++, --) have the highest precedence
Assignment operators (=, +=, etc.) have the lowest precedence and are right-associative

sections.title: Summary
sections.content: Operator precedence determines which operations happen first in expressions. Parentheses > Multiplication/Division > Addition/Subtraction. When operators have equal precedence, evaluation goes left-to-right. Practice with simple examples before tackling complex expressions - you're.

questions.question: Which operator has higher precedence: && or ||?
questions.explanation: && (logical AND) has higher precedence than || (logical OR). So in 'a || b && c', the && is evaluated first: a || (b && c).

questions.question: What does associativity determine for operators?
options: The direction of evaluation when operators have equal precedence
Whether an operator is binary or unary
The data type of the result
questions.explanation: Associativity determines the order of evaluation when operators have the same precedence. Most binary operators are left-associative (evaluated left to right), while assignment is right-associative.
